What Is Fine-Tuning?
Fine-tuning takes a pre-trained model and continues training it on a 
smaller, task-specific dataset — adapting its behavior to a particular 
domain or task.
• The model isn't trained from scratch
• It already holds general knowledge
• We only adapt it to a new, narrower task

When Should We NOT Fine-Tune?
The most overlooked question — fine-tuning isn't always the answer
You only need new knowledge
e.g., company documents
→  Use RAG instead
Knowledge changes frequently
weather, news, stock prices, inventory
→  Use RAG, not fine-tuning
Prompt engineering already works
e.g., “Translate this to French”
→  No fine-tuning needed
Your dataset is small
only ~30 examples available
→  Fine-tuning won't help much
Your budget is limited
fine-tuning still needs GPU time

Why Not Update All the Weights?
Suppose you want to fine-tune a 7B parameter model. Do you really need to update all 7 billion parameters?  No.
Full fine-tuning updates every parameter — costly in GPU memory and storage. Research shows updating only a small subset can reach similar 
performance. PEFT keeps the original weights frozen and trains only a small number of new parameters.
Full Fine-Tuning PEFT
Parameters updated All weights A few parameters
GPU memory High Low
Checkpoint size Large Small adapters
Training speed Slower Faster

T H E  M O S T  I M P O R T A N T  P E F T  M E T H O D
LoRA: The Core Idea
Instead of replacing the original weight matrix W, LoRA learns a small 
update on top of it:
W′ = W + BA
W
Original pretrained weights — frozen, untouched
A and B
Small trainable matrices — only these get updated

Sequence Length, Truncation & Padding
Every model has a maximum sequence length:
512 2048 4096 8192 128K
Truncation
Cut off tokens beyond the model's maximum sequence length.
Limit = 8  ·  Input = 12 tokens  →  keep first 8, 
discard last 4
Padding
Adds special tokens so every sequence in a batch matches in length.
"I love AI" (4 tok)  ·  "Hello" → Hello <PAD> <PAD> <PAD>
Attention Mask  — padding tokens are ignored by the model via an attention mask, so they don't affect learning.

S T E P  6  &  7
Backpropagation & the Optimizer
Backpropagation
This is where learning actually happens.
The model asks “what caused my mistake?” and calculates how 
much each trainable parameter contributed to that error — no 
manual math required to understand the idea.
Error signal flows backward
Output layer  →  Hidden layers  →  Input layer
Each parameter gets a gradient: a signal for how it should change.
Optimizer
The optimizer takes the gradients from backprop and uses them to 
update the trainable parameters.

Learning Rate — the Most Important Setting
Hyperparameters are settings we choose before training — unlike model weights, which are learned. Learning rate controls how much the model 
changes after each update.
Too Small
Slow learning — training crawls, wastes 
compute, may stall before converging.
Good
Steady, reliable improvement toward the 
best solution.
Too Large
Overshoots the best solution — loss can 
bounce or diverge.
Typical learning rate values for LLM fine-tuning 1e-5 2e-5 5e-5

Weight Decay, Warmup & Sequence Length
Weight Decay
Keeps weights from becoming 
unnecessarily large — preventing the

Learning rate ramps 0 → small →

11 Evaluation — Classification Metrics
Metrics depend on the task. For classification, these four form the core toolkit.
Accuracy
Share of all predictions the 
model got exactly right.
Precision
Of predicted positives, how 
many were actually correct.
Recall
Of actual positives, how 
many the model successfully 
found.
F1 Score
Harmonic mean of precision 
and recall — a single balance 
point.
F1 = 2 × (Precision × Recall) ÷ (Precision + Recall)

3
11 Evaluation — Generation Metrics
Open-ended text output needs different yardsticks than a fixed label set.
BLEU
N-gram precision overlap with 
reference text; standard for 
translation.
ROUGE
N-gram / sequence recall 
overlap; standard for 
summarization.
BERTScore
Embedding-based similarity 
that captures meaning, not just 
wording.
Perplexity
How well the model predicts 
held-out text — lower is more 
confident.
Human Evaluation
Automatic metrics miss fluency, factuality, and tone — human judgment remains essential, especially for generative and open-
ended tasks.
